haiku-low.q1: MySQL commits first, with its queue upsert in the same transaction, then apply_copy runs to Postgres with a 200 ms wait. A Postgres failure never fails the request; the result is ignored.
haiku-low.q2: Only when the target row's version is lower than the incoming version, and the target has no tombstone for that id. Missing rows are inserted.
haiku-low.q3: Gate 2 must pass: every web and worker instance reports build M1 and dual write on continuously for 60 s, counts match the orchestrator, and gate_dual_write_at is recorded. Instances can disagree for up to 30 s after a flag change.
haiku-low.q4: It reads 2,000 rows per batch by id, checks replica lag before and after each read (above 5 s means sleep or discard), sleeps 250 ms between batches, and holds a renewed lease.
haiku-low.q5: Reads: a clean comparison finished within 24 h, queue oldest row within SLO, no open anomalies. Source-of-truth move: 72 h at 100% reads, clean comparison within 24 h, SLO met, backups, sized Postgres, and an operator go.
haiku-low.q6: A queue row in MySQL user_sync_queue, written in the same transaction as the change, with marked_at. The sweeper copies queued users to Postgres via apply_copy, retrying until the row is safely deleted.
haiku-low.q7: Per-id lock, then a tombstone check before every copy. Erasure leaves a tombstone in users_tombstones that is never removed, so any later copy of that id stops.
haiku-low.q8: In migration_state's backfill row (owner, expires_at, last_id, done_at). The checkpoint commits in the same Postgres transaction as its batch, so restarts resume from last committed last_id. It stops when a batch is empty and sets done_at.
haiku-low.q9: Periodic comparison walks chunks of 2,000 ids and compares digests. Differing ids skipped if queued; otherwise the primary row is applied via apply_copy as a repair, or a deletion if absent. Higher Postgres version raises an alert and blocks the read ramp.
haiku-low.q10: Write source changes must pass through paused, and the tooling refuses direct changes; each instance confirms via the status endpoint. If it runs long, abort to mysql before T0+50 s; after setting pg, no abort, and restart any instance not reporting pg by T0+120 s.
haiku-low.q11: MySQL assigns ids until the switch. The Postgres sequence is then set to max(AUTO_INCREMENT, max id in both stores)+10,000,000, and creates use it. Rollback checks MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT exceeds max(id), raising it to max(id)+1 if not.
haiku-low.q12: Postgres writes apply inline to MySQL and the reverse sweeper drains them, with a daily reverse comparison. Rollback pauses, drains to empty, checks the counter, sets mysql, then reads return to 0 and a clean comparison runs. It ends at step 12 after 14 days, a clean reverse comparison, and recorded sign-off.

sonnet.q1: MySQL first (commit to the MySQL primary, with the queue row upserted in the same transaction), then apply_copy to Postgres with a 200 ms wait. If the Postgres part fails, the caller sees nothing: a Postgres failure never fails the request and the result is ignored.
sonnet.q2: Only if the incoming row's version is higher than the existing row's version (a copy may insert a missing row or replace a row whose version is lower). Also blocked if a tombstone exists for that id.
sonnet.q3: Gate 2 must pass and gate_dual_write_at must be recorded: every web and worker instance reports build M1 and users_pg_dual_write = true continuously for 60 s, with instance counts matching the orchestrator's replica count (Gate 1 before that). Instances can disagree for up to 30 s after a flag change (30 s refresh).
sonnet.q4: It reads from the replica, not the primary, in batches of up to 2,000 rows. It checks replica lag (above 5 s: sleep 5 s and recheck; a batch read during lag is discarded), and sleeps 250 ms between batches to keep replica load low for reporting jobs. It backs off exponentially on errors.
sonnet.q5: Before reads move: a clean comparison run within the last 24 h, queue oldest row within SLO, and no open anomalies (after backfill done and compare run). Before the source of truth moves: reads held at 100% for 72 h (reads_100_at + 72 h), a clean comparison within 24 h, queue age within SLO, fresh backups of both stores, Postgres sized for write load, and an operator's go decision.
sonnet.q6: The queue row in user_sync_queue (marked_at set by the write) records it. It is kept in MySQL (the source store), written in the same MySQL transaction as the write. The sweeper claims queue rows, reads the current row from the primary, and applies it to Postgres with apply_copy, then deletes the queue row if marked_at is unchanged.
sonnet.q7: Tombstones. A deletion removes the row and inserts a tombstone (users_tombstones) in one transaction in the target; every apply_copy takes a per-id lock and checks for the tombstone first and stops if one exists. Ids are never reused. The queue row also makes the sweeper apply a deletion when the source row is missing.
sonnet.q8: In Postgres migration_state, row backfill (owner, expires_at, last_id, done_at). The last_id checkpoint is committed in the same Postgres transaction as the batch of apply_copy calls. The backfill stops when a batch comes back empty: it sets done_at and releases the lease.
sonnet.q9: The comparison (hourly until the first clean run, then nightly): it compares chunk digests of 2,000 ids between replica and Postgres. For each differing id: skip if it is in the current source's queue (in flight); otherwise read from the primary and apply to Postgres via apply_copy (counted as a mismatch and repair), with a Postgres-only row applied as a deletion. If Postgres has a higher version than the primary, do not overwrite; alert and block the read ramp.
sonnet.q10: Write-source changes always pass through paused (mysql -> paused -> pg); the tooling refuses direct changes. Instances confirm via the status endpoint (reporting paused only when the in-flight count is zero), and the tooling waits for all instances rather than a fixed sleep. If it runs long: before T0+45 s the check fails, abort back to mysql (safe, no Postgres writes). After pg is set at T0+50 s it cannot be aborted; an instance not reporting pg by T0+120 s is restarted and returns 503 until then. The pause target is 90 s max (aim about 80 s).
sonnet.q11: Postgres, from its sequence users_id_seq. Each switch to pg sets the sequence during the pause to max(MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT, max(id) in both stores) + 10,000,000 and verifies it. The MySQL shadow receives rows with explicit ids, moving InnoDB's counter up. On rollback, it checks MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT is above max(id), and if not sets it to max(id) + 1, before writes return to MySQL.
sonnet.q12: In pg mode each write commits to Postgres with a Postgres queue row in the same transaction, then applies to MySQL inline (200 ms wait); the reverse sweeper drains the Postgres queue into MySQL with apply_copy, and a daily reverse comparison runs. Rollback (step 11): pause, drain the reverse queue within 45 s (abort back to pg if not drained), check AUTO_INCREMENT, set mysql at T0+50 s, start forward sweeper, poll instances, set reads back to 0, run a clean comparison. The option ends at step 12 (point of no return): at least 14 days after switching to pg, plus a clean reverse comparison, queue age within SLO and recorded sign-off, when users_write_targets = pg_only stops copying to MySQL.
